note: One tea wiki also lists Kagoshima as a growing area; the Kyoto-focused accounts do not mention it, so it was left out.

Colour values approximate a fresh-leaf dish. A further ingredient list (chilli, yellow-fruit leaf) and a local name 拉拨批皮 appeared only in an unconfirmed snippet and were left out. Heritage status not confirmed.
Could not verify anything beyond the master-list row: name, place and green category are unconfirmed.
The master list placed this in Hadong, but the located description names Boseong, so Boseong is used.
Start date of the research differs by source (1984, 1986); the appearance fields are typical of the class, not specific descriptions.
Details on grades, FAO listing and the 500-year tree come from search snippets; the full FAO page refused access.
Reading of 圩 here (xū vs wéi) is unverified; row alias suggests Diwei, so both are given.
Nearly all detail rests on one regional specialty page; 1981 and 1990 claims have no independent confirmation.
Dry leaf, liquor and taste are typical of mass-market green tea; the origin of the imported leaf is not established.
name_zh is a plain rendering of the kana name, not an established Chinese name.

name_zh is descriptive, no established Chinese name for Long Cốc. Taste, appearance and processing are typical of the region, not recorded for this tea.
The 1990s cultivation date in another source differs from the city's 1999; the city's figure is attributed.
The Hwaeomsa record and 544 date come from search snippets only.
Origin country changed from Uzbekistan to Kazakhstan; origin account rests on one page. Wikipedia title is the Russian page. Taste and brewing ratios are general.
Chinese name is a descriptive rendering. Taste notes not sourced.
The milulu page contains Ming-era tribute history, Xu Guangqi and Li Dongyang quotes that clearly belong to Lu'an Guapian with the name swapped; these and its 2011 award claim were left out.
Process rests almost entirely on one importer's account; region reflects that producer only. name_zh is a plain rendering.
Accounts differ between flat-straight and scissor-shaped description, and on pan or bake fixing.
The osmanthus-black preference comes from a search summary; the journal URL was matched to it by title and was not opened.
The master row placed this in Tongcheng; nothing read connects it to Tongcheng, so the region was changed to Shitai. The Götheborg identification rests on commercial and press accounts.
No source specific to Yunlong kao cha was found; the method is described from related Yunnan roasted teas.
Breeding origin not verified. The Fujian region rests on research use and the name, not on a stated breeding record.
Both pages are aggregator or producer-derived; award claims left out except the dated trademark.
Details come from a search snippet of the 2013 paper; the snippet did not tie the text to one specific URL, so no URL is cited.
name_zh is a descriptive rendering; no established Chinese name was confirmed.
Chinese name is a descriptive rendering. Chinese parent disputed.
Chinese name is a descriptive rendering from 藤かおり.
Category changed from heicha to green: the recorded method has no post-fermentation. Colours are estimates from modern re-creations. Wikipedia title is the Chinese page.
Unverified: the link to Anji and the pale spring leaf. Verified: a Zhejiang cultivar, and its picking order.
name_zh is descriptive. Taste and leaf appearance are typical of Thái Nguyên teas. Facts come from search snippets, not read in full.
name_zh is descriptive. Tree ages and hectare figures conflict between reports.
name_zh is a descriptive rendering; no established Chinese name was confirmed.
Could not verify anything beyond the master-list row: name, place and green category are unconfirmed.
One listing also shows a 2006 registration entry; the 2003 date is from the most detailed account. name_zh is a plain rendering, not an established Chinese name.
Dates rest on one regional specialty page.
Read from search snippets. The Ciwidey attribution and 1980s date are single-source.
Single source. It calls the tea sun-dried type yet describes re-baking; the 1945 Japanese link is uncorroborated.
Master row placed it in Yibin; the only source read ties it to Leshan, so region was changed. Category green is assumed from the row.
Only one substantive page, a tea encyclopedia site, and it equates this name with qing zhuan and chuan zi cha.
Chongqing here is 崇庆 (Chongqing County in Sichuan), not the modern city.

Kept separate because the 川 stamp has its own history, but this is the same tea family as hubei-heicha and lao-qing-cha. The 1860s timing is inferred from the merchant's career in the page, so check it.

Raw material unconfirmed: I recall mi zhuan being pressed from fine black tea dust, but nothing read supports it and the heritage description differs, so the text leaves it out. Some classifications may place it under black tea rather than heicha.
1953 and 1983 dates come from one search snippet; that page could not be opened in full. Taste and colours are typical of raw tuos.
History is backed by press citations of the old texts, not the texts themselves. Modern product details are thin.
Overlaps heavily with lao-qing-cha and chuan-zi-cha in this batch: all three names point to Hubei brick tea. Early dates conflict.

White petal, green calyx detail comes from a search snippet not tied to one URL. A seller page claims spring picking; Chinese sources point to autumn. Botanical species is general knowledge, not from the sources read.
Peru link comes only from the master list. Taste tags and appearance are inferred from the class; no direct taste report was read.
Taste is inferred from the reported currant aroma; colours are typical of dried and fermented leaf.
A brand kept as a card because it is a historic formula with its own encyclopedia page. Canned liquor colour and taste are not stated in the sources read.
Italy comes from the master list; the plant is Mediterranean-wide. Colour is typical of the class.
No dated account of early Russian home use was read.
Colours and appearance are typical of dried-leaf infusions.
Brewing and taste are class-typical, not sourced for this tea specifically. Village name in the source was rendered inconsistently (茶坑 vs Chaping); Chakeng follows the characters.
Turkey as origin kept from the master list; the tea is not specific to Turkey.
Master list said United Kingdom; earliest documented accounts are North American, so country changed.
Liquor and leaf appearance are inferred from the class of dried green-leaf infusions.
Guangxi as origin comes from the master list and was not confirmed by the sources read. Appearance and liquor are class-typical.
Colours are typical of Sideritis teas. The zh name is a descriptive rendering built on the genus name 毒马草属.
Harvest and colour notes are typical of the herb class, not specific reports.
Caffeine field is none as a plain-class judgement; the stimulant effect comes from coca alkaloids. Legal lists differ slightly between language versions.
Greek text dates Embaros cultivation to about 70 years; the IUCN gives the 1920s. Liquor colour is typical of the class.
Start date of Leão's roasted mate varies between accounts, so the text gives the range.
origin_country is a judgement call; nettle tea is traditional across all of Europe.
'Aged tea' has no English Wikipedia article (checked); 'Tea processing' used as the umbrella. The pu-erh group covers specific vintages; this card is the concept.
'Oriental Beauty' redirects to 'Dongfang meiren' on English Wikipedia (verified); used as the closest article for the style.
Card covers both Greek sage (Salvia fruticosa) and common sage (Salvia officinalis); the Wikipedia link points at the more recognisable common sage.
No dedicated English Wikipedia article for Rose Congou (title checked and missing).
origin_country is a judgement call; lemon balm tea is traditional across Europe.
origin_country is a judgement call; the methods and the approximate 97–98 % removal figure are from general knowledge and worth a fact-check.
'Scented tea' redirects to 'Tea blending and additives' on English Wikipedia, so that umbrella is used.
No dedicated English Wikipedia article for Scottish breakfast tea (the title does not exist); the soft-water origin claim is a widely repeated seller's story, not a documented fact.
origin_country is a judgement call: rosehip tea is traditional across all of Europe; Germany chosen as the strongest commercial tea tradition, with Chile and Bulgaria the main growers.
origin_country is a judgement call; elderflower tea is traditional across all of Europe.
Wikipedia title uses an en dash (Hong Kong–style milk tea), verified via the API. The intangible-heritage listing date (2017 is the usual citation) given loosely as 'the 2010s'.

EU labelling rules summarised from Regulation (EC) 1334/2008 as I understand them (the 95 % rule for 'natural X flavouring'); worth a fact-check. Origin as Germany/France is a judgement about where the modern style was industrialised.

origin_country set to Korea for the saenggang-cha tradition; ginger itself is native to Island Southeast Asia and ginger drinks are traditional across Asia and the Caribbean, so this is a judgement call.

Caffeine set to none: Ilex kudingcha is generally reported as caffeine-free or containing only traces, unlike its relatives yerba mate and guayusa; Ligustrum robustum contains none. Worth a fact-check.
The Altai (Barnaul) origin of commercial cultivation is from general knowledge; worth a fact-check.

No dedicated English Wikipedia article for the drink; 'Kapor tea' redirects to the plant article. Origin given as Russia for the historic Koporye trade; Ukrainian and Belarusian production is now significant.
A traditional style rather than a defined product; the component list is representative of commercial and homemade blends, not a standard.
origin_country given as Egypt for the karkade tradition; Sudan grows much of the crop and West Africa, Mexico and Thailand are also major sources. Harvest window is approximate.

origin_country set to Egypt because it is the dominant source of tea-grade chamomile; the plant is native to Europe and western Asia and chamomile tea is a pan-European tradition. Egyptian harvest window (Feb–Apr) given as approximate.
The late-1990s appearance of the 'gong ting' grade name is from Menghai trade history (often tied to the Menghai Tea Factory around 1999); the exact year varies by source.
The 2,700-year age of the Qianjiazhai 'No. 1' wild tea tree is the commonly quoted figure from a 1990s survey and is stated as a claim; altitude figures around 2,450 m are from the same reports.

The list of state-forest garden names and the mid-2010s start of the category are from trade reporting; regulations on picking inside protected forest have varied over time and are described only in general terms.

The recipe-number convention (year, grade, factory) and the 1975 date are standard; the '88 Qing Bing' label covers batches from roughly 1988–1992 in trade usage. The English Wikipedia article on the Menghai Tea Factory does not exist, hence the umbrella link.
The Sichuan-merchant origin of the Yibang small-leaf population is local tradition, flagged as such; elevation figures are approximate.

The closure of the original Kunming Tea Factory in the 1990s and its re-establishment in 2006 under China Tea (Zhong Cha) are from company history; the exact closure year varies by source (often given as 1994).

Elevation and the c. 2008 purchasing agreement (Chen Sheng Hao) are from general tea-trade reporting; the household count was dropped as unverifiable; the exact year the price boom began is usually given as 2007 or 2008.

UNESCO inscription of the 'Cultural Landscape of Old Tea Forests of the Jingmai Mountain in Pu'er' was in September 2023; the claim that it is the first tea-themed World Heritage site is widely reported.
The Nam Kee (Hong Kong) origin of the 8582 recipe in 1985 is standard trade history; details of the thick/thin paper variants are collector lore and dates vary slightly by source.

The Bada wild tea tree at Hesong is usually quoted as about 1,700 years old; its collapse in 2012 was widely reported. The founding decade of the factory's Bada base is given as the 1980s in company history.
Form set to 'other' (loose nuggets, also pressed into bricks). The 2006 Dayi Lao Cha Tou brick as the product that popularised the category is standard trade history.
The 1950s origin of iron cakes at Xiaguan is the usual trade account but is not well documented; the 8653 recipe is generally dated to 1986. Flag for fact-check.
The 1980s low-pruning of Mahei's old gardens is widely reported by producers and vendors who work there; the exact extent varies by garden.

Zi Juan was selected at the Yunnan Academy of Agricultural Sciences Tea Research Institute (Menghai) from a purple plant identified in 1985 according to Chinese sources; registration dates vary. Colour-change behaviour with acid/alkali is the normal anthocyanin reaction.
Dianhong's origin in 1939 at Shunning (now Fengqing) is standard tea history; the age of the Jinxiu tree is a local claim (about 3,200 years) and is presented as such.

Gedeng is the least documented of the six ancient mountains; the Qing-era 'tea king tree' is recorded in local gazetteers but its details are hazy, and hamlet names were given from trade sources. Flag for fact-check.

Era names (hao, yin, seven-sons) and the examples given are standard trade history; the '88 Qing Bing' designation refers to 7542 batches from roughly 1988–1992. Caffeine marked medium because aged tea is generally reported as gentler, though caffeine does not disappear with age.
The 'few hundred kilograms a year' figure for old-tree Mansong is a widely repeated trade estimate rather than an audited number; Qing tribute status is documented but details vary by source.
Elevation of the Mangluo gardens is usually given as roughly 750–1,000 m; the year Xigui prices took off is given variously as 2008–2010.
The remark that some 'wild' Ailao lots include non-assamica Camellia species (taliensis-type trees) is widely reported by botanists and vendors but is not universally true of every lot.

The account of Bingdao as the planting origin of the Mengku large-leaf type comes from local county records and trade lore; stated here as what records say, not as established fact. The year the price boom started is given variously as 2012–2015.

Category set to sheng because the traditional product uses sun-dried raw leaf; ripe (shu) versions are common and are covered in the text. The parent list placed this under shu, so swap the category if the catalog prefers.

English Wikipedia has a 'Chenpi' article about the peel itself, but the tea product has no article, so the pu-erh umbrella is used. The mid-2010s popularity boom of xiaoqinggan is from Chinese trade reporting.

The 1941 founding as Kangzang Tea Factory is from company history; the attribution of the tuo shape to Dali merchants (the Yongchang Xiang firm, around 1902) is the standard account but rests on trade histories rather than primary records.

The Xiao Fa tuo export to France is generally dated to 1976 via the importer Fred Kempler; the 'glutinous rice' scent comes from the leaves of a Yunnan herb (Semnostachya menglaensis), not from rice. Card covers both the full-size ripe tuo and the mini tuo as requested.

The origin of the English word 'Lapsang' is uncertain and deliberately not explained. Restrictions on pine-wood use in the Wuyi reserve are widely reported by Tongmu makers; exact rules and dates vary by account. Use of smoke flavouring in cheap export grades is reported by traders rather than documented officially.

Overview card; no English Wikipedia article exists for Anhua dark tea at time of writing ('Anhua dark tea' and variants are missing). Individual teas have their own cards (tian-jian, gong-jian, sheng-jian, fu-zhuan, hei-zhuan, hua-zhuan, qian-liang-cha). The late-2000s dark-tea boom is a widely reported market phenomenon rather than a dated event.
Naming conventions (Xiao/Da Chi Gan, Tong Jun Mei) follow Tongmu makers' usage and vary between sellers.
The 'Ju Hong' (橘红) high grade is described in Chinese tea literature as a 1930s-era Bailin specialty; details are thin and it is mentioned only in passing.
Commercial emergence dated to roughly 2013–2015 from vendor and trade accounts; no formal origin year exists. Ageing claims beyond ~5 years are maker claims.

No English Wikipedia article for Liu Bao tea exists at time of writing ('Liubao tea' / 'Liupao tea' are missing; 'Liu Bao' is a historical person). Dating of the factory cold-water piling method to the 1950s–60s follows Chinese trade histories; exact years vary.

Mid-19th-century origin and the Hankou export role are the standard Chinese tea-history account. 'Ichang' is the historical trade spelling. The Hunan Shimen inclusion in the production area follows Chinese sources.
Grade-2 leaf standard and picking description follow Chinese standards and trade descriptions; the tribute story is tradition, presented as such.

Hao Ya A/B is an export-trade grade designation rather than an official Qimen grade; mapped here to the top gongfu grades. The Chinese name 祁红毫芽 is a back-translation used by some vendors, not a traditional grade name.

The late-2000s relaunch under the Jingwei Fu Cha brand by a Xianyang company and the protected 'Jingyang Fu brick' origin follow Chinese trade reports; the 1950s halt of Jingyang production is the standard account. Raw-material sourcing varies by maker.

Companion card to liu-bao and liu-bao-aged. Lao Cha Po picking time (around Frost's Descent) and the unpiled farmhouse style follow Guangxi vendor and trade descriptions; the name_native is a descriptive composite, not an official product name.
Grade ladder (Li Cha, Te Ming, Te Ji, numbered grades) is the traditional Qimen gongfu scheme; exact cut-offs vary by factory. 1870s origin date is the commonly cited one (often given as 1875).
Mao Feng as a Keemun style became common from roughly the 1990s onward; exact origin year not stated on purpose.

A minor regional tea with thin documentation; cultivar mix and the Zhejiang/Fujian sourcing remark are generalised from Jiangsu vendor descriptions. Tang-era tea history refers to the Yangxian tribute tea, not to black tea.
Origin as 'the first black tea' and its dating (late Ming / early Qing, c. 17th century) is the conventional account; stated as such rather than as hard fact.
1915 Panama-Pacific medal is the standard trade claim; the exact award category is not verified. Origin commonly given as 1851; stated as mid-19th century.

The 'zuo se' repeated steaming-and-piling description is generalised from Ya'an makers' accounts; brick weights (500 g standard) and bundle packaging vary by factory and era. Jin Jian is the larger, coarser sibling brick and is mentioned under ya-an-zang-cha.

The night-dew ('ye lu') step and the gentle basket firing follow Chinese descriptions of the traditional method; the 1980s revival and the Sun Yi Shun brand history are from trade accounts. 'Lu'an' is the standard reading of 六安, though 'Liu An' is common in tea-shop usage.
The 1950s development for Soviet export and the Shengzhou production centre follow Chinese tea-history sources; current production figures are not documented.

'Ya'an Zang Cha' geographical indication is dated to 2008 in Chinese sources; stated as 'the 2000s'. The 'thirty-two steps' figure is a marketing claim used by Ya'an makers and is mentioned only as such.
Origin is usually given as 1874 or 'Guangxu era'; stated as 1870s. The da cha / xiao cha blending practice is traditional and not every modern maker follows it.
The Fujian-migrant origin story is the standard local account and is presented as such; cultivar mix is generalised from Hangzhou producers' descriptions.

No dedicated English Wikipedia article exists at time of writing ('Jin Jun Mei' is missing), so the Wuyi tea umbrella is used. Creation story (2005, Zhengshan Tang / Jiang Yuanxun with tea master Liang Junde) follows the most widely repeated account; bud counts per 500 g are quoted very differently by sources and are left vague.

Origin dating (Bai Liang in the Daoguang era, Qian Liang around the 1860s–70s) and the 1958 halt, 1983 and 1997 revivals follow Chinese tea-history sources; the 49-day ('seven sevens') drying period is traditional and varies with weather.
Storage-history generalisations (Malaysia, Hong Kong, Wuzhou) follow trade accounts; age claims on old Liu Bao are notoriously hard to verify and the card says so.
A Western trade name; the mapping to Tanyang/Bailin tippy grades is the usual trade explanation and the Chinese name 金猴茶 is a back-translation used by some sellers.

The claim that much Guangxi bud tea is sold as Jin Jun Mei or Yunnan tea is widely reported in the Chinese tea trade but not officially documented. Lingyun Baihao is a registered national cultivar; 1960s start of Gui Hong gongfu production follows Chinese sources.
Cultivar origin: selected 1985 at the Tea Research Institute of the Yunnan Academy of Agricultural Sciences (Menghai), per Chinese cultivar registers; stated as 'mid-1980s' to be safe.
Grade-3 leaf standard follows Chinese standards; the exact origin of the name 'sheng' (raw/coarse) is not settled and is left unexplained.
The former 'Tong Jun Mei' (copper) grade and its renaming to Chi Gan is reported by Tongmu makers; exact timeline uncertain.

No English Wikipedia article for Fu brick tea exists at time of writing ('Fuzhuan tea', 'Fu brick tea' and variants are all missing). The fungus is Eurotium cristatum, now also classified as Aspergillus cristatus. Move of production from Jingyang to Hunan in the 1950s and the roughly two-week fa hua period follow Chinese industry sources.
The 1958 origin as a replacement for Qian Liang Cha at Baishaxi and the origin of the 'flower' name follow Chinese tea-history sources.

The Zhaoliqiao factory and the 'Chuan' trademark history follow Chinese trade sources; the standard 1.7 kg weight and the face/inner two-layer construction are traditional and vary by product. Piling duration for lao qing cha ('weeks to months') is given cautiously.
Tree-age claims are vendor claims and unregulated; the card deliberately avoids stating ages as fact.

State-farm history (1950s–60s, Yunnan seed, CTC export) follows Chinese sources; current production is small and poorly documented. Cultivar name 'Hainan Daye' refers to the island's native large-leaf population.

The tribute-tea origin of the Tian Jian / Gong Jian names is local tradition, presented as such. Traditional basket sizes (large baskets of tens of kilos) versus modern 1 kg retail baskets follow Chinese trade descriptions.
Development of Xiang Luo and Jin Zhen as 'new-style Keemun' in the late 1990s follows Chinese trade and research accounts; the exact year and originator vary by source.
First production at Baishaxi in 1939–40 (credited to Peng Xianze) follows Chinese tea-history sources; the wartime-route explanation is the usual account.
Historical export role is well documented; present-day production figures are not, and the pine-drying note is from older Chinese descriptions of the style.

The 'orange candy aroma' (橘糖香) descriptor and the late-February first picking are from Chinese trade descriptions; the 1950s start of commercial production (export to the USSR) is the standard account.
Origin dating (Daoguang era, early-to-mid 19th century) follows Chinese tea-history sources; cultivar information is generalised. 'Ningchow' is the historical trade spelling.
Overview card; individual teas have their own cards (tanyang-gongfu, bai-lin-gongfu, zhenghe-gongfu, lapsang-souchong-smoked, zheng-shan-xiao-zhong-unsmoked, jin-jun-mei).
Ball weight and the steaming-and-rolling method are generalised from how Yunnan vendors describe their dragon balls; some makers roll fresh oxidised leaf before the final drying instead.

No English Wikipedia article for Yingde black tea exists at time of writing ('Yingde black tea' is missing; 'Yingde' is the city). Cultivar registration year commonly given as 1988; stated as 'the 1980s'.
Botanical identity of 'wild' trees varies by area (C. taliensis, hybrids, feral sinensis); the card hedges accordingly. Lower caffeine in taliensis is reported in the literature but varies.

The 1920s Jaipuri seed introduction, the 1936 Maolan Mountain station and the 1973 release of TTES #8 are from memory and should be checked; 'Sun Moon Lake' on Wikipedia is about the lake, hence the umbrella article.
Sanxia's mid-20th-century export green tea history is from memory; whether the farmers' association grades Longjing separately from Bi Luo Chun is not certain.
Parentage given as Tainong 8 line x Ying Zhi Hong Xin from memory of TRES cultivar notes; the 'named after Wu Zhenduo's grandmother' story is widely repeated but anecdotal.
The 2008 TRES Taitung branch origin is the commonly cited date; the exact oxidation percentage varies by producer and the 70–80% figure is a typical claim rather than a measurement.
The farm's exact garden altitude and the size of its tea plantings are approximate; the Veterans Affairs Council ownership is correct as far as I know.

Competition grade names follow the general Taiwanese farmers' association scheme; the exact tier list for the Emei and Beipu competitions should be checked. The 'named by a European queen' story is flagged as legend.
That Luye (Taitung) producers popularised GABA black in the 2010s is my understanding from Taiwanese trade coverage, not a documented date.
The Japanese origin (late 1980s, Gabaron) and the 150 mg/100 g Taiwanese threshold are from memory; the anaerobic cycle timings vary by producer. Wikipedia title 'GABA tea' should be verified.
That production started in the 2010s is approximate; a few makers may have experimented earlier. Cultivar mix varies widely by producer.

The garden-clearing timeline (leases on national forest land cancelled from roughly 2015–2016) is from memory of Taiwanese news coverage; the pass altitude is approximate. Which gardens remain in production today should be checked.
Parentage (Kyang x Keemun) and 2008 release are from memory of TRES cultivar notes; the 'pomelo flower' descriptor is the station's own.
Zhang Naimiao's two trips to Anxi are usually dated to the 1890s and 1919; I give only the period to avoid a wrong year.
The post-1999-earthquake origin story is the one Lugu producers tell and is presented as such, not as documented history.

The farm's altitude range and the size of its tea plantings are approximate; I am confident Wuling Farm sells its own high-mountain oolong but less sure how much of the market 'Wuling' tea comes from the farm itself versus neighbouring gardens.

Parentage (Burmese Assam B-607 x Taiwan wild mountain tea B-729) and the 1999 release are from memory of TRES material. I did not find a dedicated English Wikipedia article I could name with confidence, so the umbrella article is used; 'Sun Moon Lake' (the lake) exists but is not about the tea.
The Fujian origin in the 1800s is the usual account but not documented precisely; 'zhong zai' as a farmers' nickname is from memory.
Which gardens are marketed as He Huan Shan is fuzzy; the Cuifeng area of Ren'ai Township and the Highway 14A corridor are my best understanding, and the 1,700–2,200 m range is approximate.
The Chiayi County 'Alishan high mountain tea' certification mark exists but I am not certain of its launch year, so no date is given.
The 2000s Ruisui origin and the farmers' association evaluation are from memory; the cultivar mix on the Wuhe terrace (Da Ye oolong dominant) is my best understanding.
The Muzha chance-seedling origin is the standard account; the name of the farmer credited with finding it is not given because I am not certain of it.
The Nantou County aged-tea evaluation is mentioned from memory without a start year; the 'two schools' (periodic re-roasting vs sealed storage) is the trade's own framing.
Lugu competition grade names and the 300 g (half-jin) pack convention are from memory of the Farmers' Association system; worth checking the current tier list.
Parentage (Ying Zhi Hong Xin x Tainong 80 line) and the 'named after Wu's mother' story are from memory; the ginger-lily / betel-flower aroma description follows TRES cultivar notes.

Botanical status (Camellia sinensis f. formosensis, sometimes treated as Camellia formosensis) and the 2019 release of TTES #24 Shan Yun from Yongkang material are from memory; the list of wild populations is approximate. Category set to black because that is how most of it is sold.

The Song-dynasty dating is traditional; the Li Zai Ping mother tree is usually described as roughly 600 years old and of the Huang Zhi Xiang type. Reports about the health or death of individual mother trees vary and are not stated here.
The rainstorm and lawsuit story (usually dated to around 1919) is told as history in Wuyi but is presented here as a story.
Yu Gui (玉桂) is an older name for the same cultivar. The Qing-dynasty record and the 1980s spread are the standard account in Chinese tea literature.

Two traditional origin accounts exist (Hui Yuan Yan below Huoyan Peak, and the Wen Gong temple at Wuyi Palace); both are given as tradition. The low-chlorophyll description of the cultivar is from Chinese cultivar literature.
Listed among the ten classic aroma types; the mother-tree site is not stated because sources differ.
The statement that the Li Zai Ping Song Zhong tree is of the Huang Zhi Xiang type follows the usual Chaozhou account.
The Fumei / Daping origin and the early-twentieth-century date (around 1907 is usually cited) follow the traditional Anxi account.
The identification of Tong Tian Xiang as the Jiang Hua Xiang mother tree in Zhong Ping, Wudong, follows Chaozhou tea sources; the tree's age (often given as 400 years or more) is traditional.

Selection in the early 1980s and provincial registration in the 1990s (1996 is usually cited) follow Chinese cultivar records; the Daqin Mountain reference is from Pinghe county tourism and tea sources.
The Beiyuan tribute-tea history of Jianou is well documented; the separate trade categorisation of Minbei versus Wuyi Shui Xian follows Chinese standards and vendor practice.

The zhengyan / banyan / zhoucha / wai shan tiers are trade conventions, not regulated grades; the national Wuyi rock tea standard defines a much broader geographic area. The list of three pits and two gullies is the standard one.

The Wikipedia article covers both the Yongchun and the Wuyi versions, hence exact scope. Xue Li as the Wuyi name for Fo Shou is the standard local usage; the citron-grafting origin is a legend and is flagged as such.
Parentage, Mingke No. 2 and number 105 from Chinese cultivar lists; often confused with Jin Guan Yin (Mingke No. 1 / 204) in vendor copy.

The Anxi Lutian origin is the traditional account in Chinese cultivar literature; the claim that much Jin Jun Mei-style black tea uses Mei Zhan leaf is common trade knowledge rather than a documented statistic.
The Jianyang origin (Zhuxian cave, Daoguang era) is the traditional account repeated in Chinese sources; the exact date of introduction to Wuyi is not firmly documented.

Tree age and the name story are traditional. Some sellers use Tong Tian Xiang and Jiang Hua Xiang interchangeably; here Tong Tian Xiang is treated as the mother-tree lineage and Jiang Hua Xiang as the aroma type, which is the usual Chaozhou distinction.

The 1960s breeding in Zhao'an (usually credited to Zheng Zhaoqin, 1965) and the 1994 national registration follow Chinese cultivar records; the exact parentage is given inconsistently in sources, so none is stated.

The Yao Yueming propagation account (1950s–60s, Bei Dou Peak) is standard in Chinese tea literature. The genetic relationship to the Da Hong Pao mother trees is disputed; Qi Dan is more often cited as the match.

Parentage (Tieguanyin × Huang Dan), the Mingke No. 1 name, number 204 and the 2002 national registration are from Chinese cultivar lists; worth a fact-check against the Huang Guan Yin entry (Mingke No. 2 / 105), as the two are often mixed up.
Named single trees of this type on Wudong are often cited in Chaozhou sources; none are named here to avoid unverifiable claims.
The identity of Wuyi Qi Lan with the Pinghe Bai Ya Qi Lan cultivar is the usual trade explanation; older local Qi Lan strains exist in Minnan and Wuyi and the labelling is not consistent.
Age thresholds for lao cong versus gao cong vary between vendors (30, 50 or 60 years are all quoted); there is no regulated definition.
The Yaoyang / Xiping origin and the circa 1870 date are from the traditional Anxi account.
The Shuangji mountain area of Raoping (Shuangji Niang Shan, around 1,000 m) is cited in Chinese sources as the county's high-elevation tea zone; production share figures are deliberately not given.
Listed among the ten classic aroma types in Chaozhou sources; the mother-tree site is not stated because sources differ.
Ju Duo Zai is treated here as the main Xing Ren Xiang clone, as it is in most Chaozhou and vendor sources; some sellers list it as a separate strain.
The original cliff site of the Jin Suo Chi mother bushes is given differently in different Chinese sources, so no site is named here.
Reproduced from the SCHEMA.md example card with minor additions to aliases.
The Luoyan / Hutou origin and the mid-nineteenth-century dating follow the traditional Anxi account.
The three-years-medicine saying is folklore. Age brackets and the chen suan description reflect common trade usage rather than any standard.
The citron-grafting story is legend. The geographical-indication status and the Southeast Asian export tradition are as commonly reported in Chinese sources.

The three-tier dancong / lang cai / shui xian grading is the traditional Chaozhou system as described in Chinese sources; the national cultivar listing of Fenghuang Shui Xian (1985) is from Chinese cultivar records.
The DNA-matching claim is widely reported in Chinese tea media; the number of distinct genotypes among the six mother trees is given variously (often three or four).
The tuberose identification of ye lai xiang follows the common Chinese usage of the plant name; the mother-tree site is not stated because sources differ.
Yu Lan Xiang is listed among the ten classic Fenghuang aroma types in Chaozhou sources; the mother-tree location is not stated here because sources disagree.
The 1980s selection from Da Hong Pao seedlings is the usual account from the Wuyi tea research institute; exact dates vary between sources.
The duck-shit-soil naming story is folklore; the Ping Keng Tou origin and the official renaming to Yin Hua Xiang (reported in the 2010s) follow Chaozhou sources.
The 1910s origin in Shuangyang township (usually dated 1914 and credited to a maker named Deng Guanjin) follows the standard local account; square size and weight vary by maker (8–12 g).
Listed among the ten classic aroma types in Chaozhou sources; no specific mother-tree site is given because sources differ.

Parentage (Tieguanyin × Huang Dan) and trade number 220 from Chinese cultivar lists; registration dates vary between provincial (2003) and national (2010) listings and are given here only as the 2000s.

The chen xiang type with a five-year minimum was added to the Anxi Tieguanyin national standard in the mid-2010s (2016 is the year usually cited); worth confirming. The stomach-remedy use is folklore.
Se Chung is the older export spelling. The description of the old Anxi grading split (Tieguanyin versus se zhong) follows Chinese trade sources.
Parentage (Huang Guan Yin × Huang Dan) and the early-2000s release are from Chinese cultivar lists and the Wikipedia stub; the trade number sometimes quoted for it (506) is not confirmed here.
Oxidation percentages are rough trade figures. The 2006 end of picking from the Jiulongke mother trees is widely reported; blend composition varies by maker.
The 1961 selection and 2002 national cultivar registration follow Chinese cultivar records; the protected-name status for Lingtou Dancong tea is as reported in Chinese sources.
English Wikipedia has no dancong article (Dancong redirects to Oolong). The Wudong origin of the Mi Lan Xiang mother tree follows Chaozhou tea sources.
The Gui Dong / Hui Yuan Keng origin is the standard account; the Song-dynasty dating is legend and is described as such.

Oxidation figures are trade approximations. The qing xiang / nong xiang split in the Anxi Tieguanyin standard (GB/T 19598) is as generally reported; the timeline of the green style's dominance (1990s–2000s) is approximate.
The Sanhua Peak cliff story and the three spellings are the standard Wuyi account, given here as folklore.
Age thresholds for lao cong vary between sellers (50, 60, 80 or 100 years are all quoted); there is no regulated definition. Elevation figures for Wudong (roughly 1,000–1,400 m) are approximate.
Da Wu Ye is variously said to originate on Wudong or elsewhere in the Fenghuang range; no specific village is stated.
The Qu Zai Liao mother tree at Li Zai Ping and the eight-cuttings story follow Chaozhou tea sources and are presented as a story.
The GI rules for Yame dentō hon gyokuro (natural straw shading, hand picking, naturally grown bushes, minimum shading period) are summarised without quoting the exact day count.
English Wikipedia article is believed to be titled 'Mecha (tea)'; if it does not exist, use 'Japanese tea' as umbrella.
English Wikipedia title assumed to be 'Yabukita'; if absent, use 'Japanese tea' as umbrella. Selection year 1908 and registration 1953 are the usual dates given.
History of the style (post-war Shizuoka, Makinohara/Kakegawa) is as commonly told in the Japanese trade; exact decade varies by source.
Card covers the brief's 'Uji sencha / Uji matcha' as one region card centred on matcha, with sencha and gyokuro as aliases. English Wikipedia title assumed to be 'Uji tea'.
Depends on the 'Benifuuki' English Wikipedia article existing; otherwise use 'Japanese tea' as umbrella.

The export-origin story of steamed guricha (early 20th century, Russian/Soviet market) is widely repeated in the trade; stated vaguely here.
The 1920s Kyoto origin is the commonly repeated trade story, presented as such.
English Wikipedia is believed to have a short 'Konacha' article; if not, use 'Japanese tea' as umbrella.
Production ranking versus Shizuoka varies by year and metric (volume vs value); the Chiran-cha brand unification across Minamikyushu city is dated 'a few years ago' rather than to a specific year.
English Wikipedia title assumed to be 'Sayama tea'; if absent, use 'Japanese tea' as umbrella.
No dedicated English Wikipedia article is known; umbrella used. The 'single household' low point is as commonly reported by Japanese sources on the revival.

English Wikipedia is believed to have a 'Batabatacha' article; if not, use 'Japanese tea' as umbrella. Mould-only (no lactic stage) fermentation and the Birudani hamlet are as described in Japanese sources on Toyama kurocha.
'Genmai-matcha' from the brief is treated as the same product as matcha-iri genmaicha and merged into this card as an alias.
Form set to 'other' because the tea is sold as small compressed tiles rather than loose leaf or a true brick. Number of producers is given as 'a handful' without a figure.

English Wikipedia title assumed to be 'Benifuuki'; if absent, use 'Japanese tea' as umbrella. Parentage (Benihomare x an Assam-derived line) and 1993 registration are the usual published details; no health claims are made beyond 'studied'.
Production share ('roughly a third') is approximate; Shizuoka and Kagoshima have traded the top spot in recent statistics.
Name and characters unverified; no page names this tea. Check against 《潮州凤凰茶树资源志》, and whether it is a variant of 蛤古 or 蝴蟆叶.
Facts from search snippets of FAAS tea papers; the exact paper URL could not be matched to each claim, so none listed.

The origin date differs between the en (about 2010) and zh (2002) pages; both are reported. Romanised chain name 盖不同 as Gai Bu Tong is my own rendering.
name_zh is descriptive; 柠檬 strictly means lemon, and the zh page uses 柠檬茶 for this drink.
Only one consumer article names this tea; it calls it one of China's ten famous teas, which is not repeated as fact. Black-tea class comes from the master list and was not independently confirmed.

Sources differ on detail: Popov's start is given as the 1890s or 1893. Lau Jon Jau's name is a transliteration from Russian. name_zh is a descriptive rendering.
Origin accounts conflict (the ja page credits Chun Shui Tang's owner and 1983; the ru page says early 1980s); the card reports the two main claims.

Founding date conflicts (1940 vs 1947); smallholder counts vary from 600 to 6,500, so the text says thousands, following the fuller estate guide. name_zh is a descriptive rendering, not an established name. Auction records seen in search snippets only.

Grade numbers follow the usual export numbering (41022 as the top grade); minor codes vary between exporters.

Cultivar card. Origin dates ('1800s and early 1900s') follow local records as usually cited (Fuding Dabai c. 1857, Fuding Dahao c. 1880s, Zhenghe Dabai c. 1880s); the national registration numbers Huacha 1 and 2 are as commonly given.
Grade card rather than a distinct tea; overlaps with xihu-longjing by design. Exact Qingming and Grain Rain dates shift by a day or two each year.

No dedicated English Wikipedia article found. The Tang tribute-workshop history is well documented in Chinese sources; the 1970s revival date follows the usual account.
Filed as white because that is how it is sold, but many lots use a green-processed bud base, as the card explains.
The etymology (xi chun / yu qian) follows the usual account; the Boston Tea Party cargo lists Hyson among the teas destroyed.
No dedicated English Wikipedia article found. Caffeine marked high because large-leaf assamica is generally higher in caffeine than sinensis greens.
The 1968 Baiqin factory origin is the standard Chinese account; not independently verified.
No dedicated English Wikipedia article found. The tasting claim about selenium is flagged as marketing.

The Wikipedia 'Thai tea' article is about the drink (cha yen) rather than the tea leaf; it is the closest umbrella. The claim that some commercial mixes use imported Ceylon/Assam leaf is based on ingredient lists and trade knowledge rather than a single source. Taste tag 'spicy' refers to the spiced commercial mixes.

No dedicated English Wikipedia article for Krasnodar tea was found ('Krasnodar tea' and 'Krasnodar Tea' both missing), so 'Russian tea culture' is the umbrella; 'Dagomys' is the alternative. Koshman's 1901 planting at Solokh-Aul is well documented; the planted area ('a few hundred hectares') and the consumer-test findings about adulterated brands are from Russian press reports and should be treated as approximate.
Founding year 1929 and founder J.A. Russell are from memory. Bharat/Cameron Valley is mentioned as the second producer; its estate details are not given.

The exact method by which Gorreana fixes its green tea (steam versus dry heat) is not stated precisely by the estate in sources I trust, so the card says only 'heated'. 'Hysson' as the estate's green grade name is from its own product range.

First plantings in the 1880s follow the Wikipedia article on tea growing in Azerbaijan; Soviet-era expansion and post-1991 decline are from general history. Azerçay blending local with imported leaf is widely reported but the proportions are not public. Taste tag 'bitter' refers to the strong style as usually brewed.

Category set to 'black' because balhyocha is usually sold as a near-fully-oxidised tea; some catalogues file it under 'yellow' together with hwangcha. The hwangcha/balhyocha distinction is a producer convention, not a regulated one.

Founding details (Chen family, cuttings imported in the 1990s, first commercial release around 2009) are from memory of press coverage and the estate's own history. Cultivar makeup beyond Qingxin is not published in detail.
Amorepacific's Seogwang garden planting dates (late 1970s to early 1980s) are from memory. Jeju as the 'second' region after Boseong by output is approximate; some sources rank Hadong second.

No dedicated Georgian tea article on English Wikipedia; 'Green tea' used as the umbrella. The history of the numbered Soviet green grades and the claim that modern 'No. 95' is largely non-Georgian are from trade knowledge and should be checked.

Dates (Hall's purchase in 1987, Bigelow partnership in 2003, Lipton's 1960s farm) and the 'Green Giant' harvester are from memory of the farm's own history and press coverage. The farm was renamed from 'Charleston Tea Plantation' to 'Charleston Tea Garden' in 2020; the Wikipedia title reflects the current name.

The 828 planting is from the Samguk Sagi; the precise location in Hwagae is a local claim. FAO GIAHS designation of the 'Traditional Hadong Tea Agrosystem' in 2017 is stated from memory; worth a quick check.

The English Wikipedia 'Hwangcha' title redirects to 'Yellow tea', which has a Korean section; 'Korean tea' would be the alternative umbrella. Category 'yellow' follows the Korean name; by process it is closer to oolong/black and some catalogues file it under oolong. Hwangcha vs balhyocha terminology is not standardised among producers.
Export destinations (Pakistan, Taiwan, Russia) reflect the usual rankings in Vietnamese trade statistics for black tea and may shift year to year. PH1 as the common estate clone is from memory.

Daejak is sometimes described as the May pick and jungjak as the June pick depending on the source; I follow the common ordering ujeon → sejak → jungjak → daejak with daejak being the latest and coarsest. The claim that late leaf goes mostly into bags/blends is general industry practice rather than a documented statistic.
Boseong green tea as Korea's first registered geographical indication (2002) is from memory. 'Largest tea-growing county' is widely stated; the exact share of national output varies by source.

Thai green tea is a small, loosely defined product and this card generalises across several Chiang Rai farms; the existence of Japanese-style steamed lots is based on farm offerings seen in the trade. The umbrella article chosen is the Mae Salong village article rather than a tea article, since no Thai green tea article exists.
Korean black tea is a small, loosely defined category; which producers make 'hongcha' versus 'balhyocha' changes from year to year, so the card describes the style rather than specific brands.

Tree ages and altitudes are as commonly claimed by producers; the 'Hà Giang Shan Tuyết' geographical indication is from memory. The cross-border trade of Vietnamese old-tree leaf into Yunnan is widely reported in the tea trade but hard to quantify.

Founding year 1883 and the Gago da Câmara family are from the estate's own history; the ages of the machinery are as stated by the estate (nineteenth-century Marshall equipment). The 'no pesticides' claim is the estate's and is credible given the climate but is not a third-party certification.
Bảo Lộc as the main scenting centre is from trade knowledge; northern makers also scent jasmine tea. Trà lài vs trà nhài is a regional naming difference rather than two products.

No dedicated English Wikipedia article was found for Georgian tea (titles 'Georgian tea', 'Tea in Georgia (country)', 'Tea production in Georgia' all missing at check time), so the generic 'Black tea' umbrella is used; 'Chakvi' or 'Agriculture in Georgia (country)' are the alternatives. Liu Junzhou's dates and the 1830s first plantings are from memory; the Paris 1900 exhibition medal often cited for Chakvi tea is deliberately omitted.

No dedicated Wikipedia article on Argentine tea was found; the province article is used as the umbrella. Planting history (1920s seed, 1950s expansion) and INTA's role at Cerro Azul are from memory. The United States as the main export destination for iced tea is well established in trade reporting.

No dedicated Iranian tea article found on English Wikipedia ('Iranian tea' missing; 'Tea in Iran' redirects to 'Iranian cuisine'); the 'Lahijan' city article is used as the umbrella. Kashef al-Saltaneh's introduction of tea around 1900 and the Indian origin of the stock are well-known history but dates are approximate. The scale of imported/smuggled tea is widely reported but unquantified here.

Cultivar identity is the main uncertainty: Thai 'No. 17 / Ruan Zhi' is sold as one cultivar, while Taiwanese numbering gives No. 17 as Bai Lu and 'Ruan Zhi' as a name for Qing Xin. The card describes the Thai product as sold and flags the confusion.
The reported practice of Vietnamese oolong being sold as Taiwanese is widely covered in trade press and Taiwanese media but not quantified here. Altitude range and harvest counts are approximate.

Hawaiian tea is a loose category of small-farm teas and the card describes typical oolongs rather than a single product. The 'Hawaii-grown' labelling rule (requiring 100% Hawaii-grown leaf for that label) is from memory and should be checked. Numbers of farms and elevations are approximate.

Brand line names (Rize Turist, Filiz, Tiryaki, Altınbaş) are Çaykur products as remembered; the geographical-indication status and the Georgian origin of the planting stock are from memory. Pesticide-free status is commonly claimed on the basis of the cold winters, not a certification.
Kayu Aro planting date (1920s) and altitude are from memory; 'one of the largest contiguous plantations' is a commonly made claim. Sumatra oolong production is small and the description is general.

Cross-border sale of Vietnamese leaf as Yunnan pu-erh is widely reported in the trade but not quantified. Cao Bồ's organic certification is from memory. Ageing behaviour of Vietnamese cakes is genuinely not well documented; the card says so.

No dedicated English Wikipedia article for miang (the 'Miang' title redirects elsewhere), so 'Fermented tea' is the umbrella. The names 'miang fad' (astringent, short fermentation) and 'miang som' (sour, long fermentation) are given as commonly used; spellings vary. Category 'heicha' is the best fit for a post-fermented tea that is eaten; fermentation times are approximate.

Altitude, founding decade (1970s) and the organic/pesticide-free claim are from the producer's own marketing and general reporting; treat the organic claim as the garden's claim. The 'Sabah Tea' Wikipedia article is about the company, hence 'umbrella'.
Dates (Assam seed in the 1870s, Malabar founded by Bosscha in the 1890s) are from memory and approximate. Clone series names (GMB, TRI) are given generally; the dominant clones vary by estate.

First planting (1999) and first sale (2005) are from memory of press coverage. The proportion of Cornish leaf in the estate's blends is not published and is described only as 'a small share'. Scottish tea growers were considered for a separate card and omitted for lack of confidence after the publicised fraud case involving one 'Scottish tea' supplier.

'Malcha' on English Wikipedia is a disambiguation page, so the umbrella 'Matcha' article is used. Shading practices vary by producer; the statement that Korean malcha is generally shaded less is a generalisation from producer descriptions.

Dates for the introduction of Taiwanese cultivars to Mae Salong (late 1980s to 1990s) and the altitude range are approximate. 'No. 12' corresponds to the Taiwan Tea Research and Extension Station cultivar number for Jin Xuan.

Daintree Tea Company planting date (late 1970s) and the Cutten brothers' Bingil Bay plantings (1880s) are from memory. Tasmanian tea growing is mentioned only as small-scale and is the least certain claim; no specific Tasmanian producer is named.
Flower counts per kilogram (often quoted as around 1,000) vary by source and are given only as 'many hundreds'. The number of scenting rounds (5–7) is the commonly described traditional range.

No Wikipedia article for Bitaco or Colombian tea was found; 'Black tea' is used as the generic umbrella. Planting decade (1960s), altitude and the origin of the plant material are from the estate's own history and press coverage and should be checked. Ecuador's small tea industry (Sangay) was considered and omitted for lack of confidence.

Grade names and their picking standards (đinh, nõn tôm, móc câu) are common trade usage rather than a regulated standard. Trung du as the traditional cultivar and the newer clones are from memory; Tân Cương has a geographical indication but the registration year is not stated here.

Form set to 'cake' for pressed coins; 'other' would also fit. The 'green moss' bloom and microbial ageing are the traditional account; modern commercial cheongtaejeon is sometimes dried more quickly and may show little fermentation. Tteokcha is also used by some producers for larger pressed cakes, hence the combined name.

Brand names are given as examples of major Central Java jasmine tea producers; founding details are deliberately omitted. The 'wasgitel' acronym is a well-known Tegal saying about teh poci; its spelling varies between sources.

Vietnamese white tea is a small, young category; descriptions reflect typical specialty lots from Hà Giang and Yên Bái cooperatives rather than a standardised product. Ageing practice follows the Chinese white-tea model and is a trade habit, not a regulation.

Burmese script for 'laphet chauk' and the teashop term 'yay nway gyan' are given from memory and should be checked for spelling. The 'Lahpet' article covers Burmese tea culture broadly and is used as the umbrella; no dedicated Myanmar green tea article exists. The export of Myanmar dry tea to China is widely reported but unquantified.

Category 'heicha' chosen because laphet is a microbially post-fermented tea leaf product; 'other' would be the alternative. Fermentation times are the commonly stated range (months); some producers use shorter or longer pickling.

No Lao-script name given (the generic Lao word for tea is 'saa'; a specific native product name is not established). Tree ages at Ban Komaen (often quoted as 400+ years) are local claims. The share of Lao leaf sold into Yunnan is widely reported in the tea trade but unquantified. Category 'sheng' chosen because the product is made and sold as raw pu-erh style; 'Pu'er tea' would be the alternative umbrella article.
Cake form inferred from the 357 g weight of the 2023 edition; the form of the 2008 100 g lot is not stated.

No Wikipedia article on Malawian tea, so 'Black tea' is used as umbrella ('Shire Highlands' and 'Thyolo District' exist but are not tea articles). Clone series names (SFS, PC) and the Limbe auction detail are from memory.
Kenyan white tea is a small niche; the producing areas and 'couple of decades' history are from memory and worth a check.

Native name in Bengali for the Dooars only. No dedicated tea article on Wikipedia; the regional article is used as umbrella.
Arunachal's tea industry is young and documentation is thin; planting dates and the Donyi Polo estate details are from memory. No Wikipedia article on Arunachal tea.

Sinhala spelling of Dimbula and the estate names are from memory.
No Wikipedia article on Tanzanian tea; 'Black tea' used as umbrella ('Agriculture in Tanzania' and 'Usambara Mountains' exist). Estate details from memory.

'Moonlight' is a marketing name used by several estates (Castleton, Jungpana, Goomtee, Margaret's Hope) for very light AV2 first-flush lots, not a defined grade; category set to black because it is sold as a first-flush black tea even though it is barely oxidised.
